Digital Image Processing — Exam Guide 3
1 Introduction, Pipeline, Imaging Modalities, Sensors
1.1 What is Digital Image Processing (DIP)?
A digital image is a continuous light signal converted into a pixelated matrix. DIP means pro￾cessing those matrices with algorithms: mostly image-in, image-out operations (enhancement,
filtering, restoration, compression).
DIP vs. Computer Vision (CV): DIP transforms an image into a better image. CV extracts
meaning from an image (recognise, detect, decide).
Step Belongs to
Original selfie Input
Increase brightness DIP
Remove noise DIP
Detect face DIP / CV boundary
Recognise person Computer Vision
Unlock phone Computer Vision
1.2 Image Formation Model
f(x, y) = i(x, y) r(x, y), 0 < i(x, y) < ∞, 0 < r(x, y) < 1
where i(x, y) is illumination and r(x, y) is reflectance.
Pipeline: Illumination → Reflection f(x, y, λ) → Optical lens → Sensor plane f(x, y) → Sam￾pling f(i, j) → Quantization q(i, j) → Digital image g(i, j) → Encoding / Storage / Transmis￾sion.

3 Intensity Transformations, Contrast, Histograms
3.1 Basic Definitions
 Contrast: variation in the intensity of pixels.
 Tones: variation in brightness/contrast/colour across an image — highlights, midtones,
shadows.
 Negative: inverts intensity levels.
 Diapositive: identity transform (positive transparency).
Negative (8-bit): s = 255 − r General: s = (L − 1) − r Diapositive: s = r
3.2 Reading a Histogram
x-axis = intensity (0–255), y-axis = frequency. Mass near 0 = dark image; mass near 255
= bright image. Narrow histogram = low contrast; wide spread = high contrast. Higher
variance of the intensity distribution means higher contrast.
3.3 Contrast Shifting vs. Stretching
Shifting: adding a constant moves all values equally (contrast unchanged, brightness changes).
Stretching: expands the intensity range.

5 Colour: False Colour Composites and HSV
5.1 False Colour Composite (FCC)
A colour image built by assigning spectral bands (including wavelengths beyond the visible
spectrum, e.g. NIR) to the R, G, B display channels.
#composites = 3! = 6, #true colour = 1, #false colour = 3! − 1 = 5
Standard remote-sensing FCC: NIR→R, Red→G, Green→B, so healthy vegetation appears
bright red (vegetation reflects IR strongly).
Why HSV is used: separately equalizing R, G, B distorts colour balance. Converting to HSV
and equalizing only V (brightness) keeps hue and saturation intact.

6.3 Moore Neighbour Tracing
Traces the boundary of a binary object clockwise using the 8 surrounding (Moore) neighbours.
Produces a boundary coordinate list.
Procedure: (1) find first object pixel, (2) note the backtrack pixel, (3) examine 8 neighbours
clockwise from backtrack, (4) move to first object pixel found, update backtrack, (5) stop at
start pixel.

Digital Image Processing — Exam Guide 15
6.5 Hough Transform
Isolates straight lines and circles in a binary edge map using a global voting procedure in
parameter space; robust to broken/noisy edges.
ρ = x cos θ + y sin θ
ρ = perpendicular distance from origin, θ = angle of that perpendicular.
Algorithm: (1) each point (x, y) maps to a sinusoid in (ρ, θ) space; (2) accumulator array
counts votes; (3) each edge pixel votes for all (ρ, θ) lines through it; (4) peaks in the accumulator
give detected lines.
